comparison: Both strongly support the central finding that cerebellum (not basal ganglia) is critical for DYT1 dystonia. OpenEval cites comprehensive experimental evidence (C3, C19, C128, C146) while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as 'novel and important' and note it 'challenges decades of focus on the basal ganglia.' Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with no concerns raised.

Both address basal ganglia knockdown findings (C24-C30). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by Western blot, histology, and behavioral data. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the core anatomical comparison, with no concerns raised about the basal ganglia control experiments.

Both address cerebellar knockdown producing dystonia (C31-C39). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by multiple lines of evidence including Western blots, histology, behavioral scoring, and EMG. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm these findings as novel and important without raising concerns.

Both evaluate dose-response relationship (C40-C43). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by correlation analysis showing 60% knockdown threshold. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting additional physiological analysis of animals with low knockdown/no dystonia to validate the correlation, suggesting the relationship needs further experimental support.

Both address DCN firing abnormalities (C44-C54). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by in vivo recordings with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting correlation between physiological findings and behavioral phenotype severity, indicating the link between physiology and behavior needs strengthening.

Both evaluate Purkinje cell firing irregularity (C56-C61). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by in vivo recordings. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting correlation with phenotype severity and recordings from animals with varying knockdown levels to establish mechanistic link between Purkinje cell and DCN dysfunction.

Both address Purkinje cell intrinsic excitability (C64-C70). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by in vitro recordings with strong internal controls (GFP+ vs GFP-). Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging these findings provide mechanistic insight into 'abnormal intrinsic excitability' with implicit acceptance of the GFP comparison.

Both evaluate DCN intrinsic excitability (C72-C76). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by in vitro recordings paralleling Purkinje cell experiments. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging these mechanistic findings as part of understanding 'potential mechanism' through 'abnormal intrinsic excitability.' No specific concerns raised.

Both address cell death findings (C80-C85). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED but notes caution about interpretation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising multiple concerns: inadequate sample size (N=3), high baseline TUNEL staining in controls (5-10%), and lack of correlation with behavioral phenotype. Reviewers consider this 'important finding' requiring more rigorous validation.

Both evaluate age-dependent effects and developmental compensation (C90-C92, C4, C21, C129). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by juvenile injection experiments. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging this as key evidence for compensation hypothesis and central to manuscript's impact on understanding why transgenic models fail.

Both address compensation hypothesis (C4, C21, C129). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by juvenile experiments showing lack of dystonia despite adequate knockdown. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting this addresses 'remarkable developmental component' of human disorder and explains transgenic model failures.

Both address background claims about DYT1 genetics and clinical features (C1, C6, C7) and prior model failures (C2, C10-C13). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by literature citations. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging the historical context without questioning these established facts.

Both address prior genetic model failures (C2, C10-C13). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by extensive literature citations establishing rationale for current approach. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'animal models have not been particularly reflective of the human disease.'

Both address species differences in torsinA expression (C14-C16). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by expression studies, noting compensation hypothesis is reasonable. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging speculation about 'developmental compensation different from humans.'

Both address neuroimaging literature on cerebellar involvement (C8, C9). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED, noting current study provides causal evidence that imaging cannot. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this background context as part of their acknowledgment of the manuscript's contribution to understanding cerebellar dystonia.

OpenEval addresses non-significant trends in DCN firing (C52, C53) as SUPPORTED, appropriately describing trends rather than significant findings. Peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating for broader DCN physiology (R3) includes request for phenotype correlation but doesn't specifically challenge the reporting of these trends.
